items.proof_outline: Since cos 2θ = 2cos²θ - 1, the expression equals 2(1 + cos θ)², a square times 2.

Each summand is non-negative, so the product has modulus at least 1. A zero at 1+it gives a factor of order (σ-1)^4 against a pole of order (σ-1)^{-3} and a bounded factor, so the product tends to 0, contradicting the lower bound.
Each factor has modulus at most 1/(1 - 2^{-σ}) and at least 1/(1 + p^{-σ}) > 0; since Σ p^{-σ} converges, the log of the product converges, so the product is the exponential of a finite number.
ξ(-2n) = ξ(1+2n) is finite. In the defining product, Γ(s/2) has a simple pole at s = -2n while the other factors are finite and nonzero, so ζ(-2n) must vanish to keep ξ finite.
The Fourier series x = Σ 2(-1)^{n+1} sin(nx)/n on (-π, π) and Parseval's identity give (1/π)∫_{-π}^{π} x² dx = 2π²/3 = Σ 4/n², hence Σ 1/n² = π²/6.
For s > 1, 1/(s-1) ≤ ζ(s) ≤ 1 + 1/(s-1) by comparison with the integral; multiply by s - 1 and let s → 1+.
On Re(s) ≥ σ₀ > 1 the terms are bounded by n^{-σ₀}, a convergent series; the Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence and the limit is holomorphic.
Hardy's argument: if Z had finitely many sign changes, |∫_T^{2T} Z| = ∫_T^{2T} |Z| for large T, but the first integral is O(T^{7/8}) while the second is ≫ T.
Argument principle on the rectangle with vertices -1, 2, 2+iT, -1+iT; Stirling for arg of π^{-s/2}Γ(s/2); Jensen-type bound for the number of zeros near 1/2+iT gives S(T) = O(log T).
Truncated Perron formula with c > 1, shift to Re(s) = -U, residues at s = 1, at each ρ, at s = 0 and at the trivial zeros; let U → ∞ and the height T → ∞ along a sequence avoiding zeros.
Mertens-type inequality from 3 + 4cos + cos2 ≥ 0, then -Re ζ'/ζ(s) < A log t - Σ_ρ Re 1/(s-ρ) bounds; isolate the term from the putative zero and pick σ = 1 + δ/log t.
Robin's direction: under RH explicit Chebyshev bounds control Π_{p≤x} (1-1/p)^{-1}; the extremal n are colossally abundant and are checked against the bound, small cases by computation.
If RH fails, oscillation (Ω) results for θ(x) - x with an exponent b > 1/2 make σ(n) ≥ e^γ n log log n for infinitely many colossally abundant n (Robin, building on Nicolas).

For large n, exp(H_n) log H_n = e^γ n log log n + (positive term of order n/log n) + smaller terms, so Robin's inequality for n > 5040 implies the harmonic-number inequality there; n ≤ 5040 is checked directly. Conversely, if RH fails, σ(n) exceeds e^γ n log log n by far more than that gap for infinitely many n (Robin), so the harmonic-number inequality fails too.
For ρ = 1/2 + iγ, |1 - 1/ρ| = 1, so 1 - (1-1/ρ)^n has real part 1 - cos(nθ_ρ) ≥ 0; summing over zeros gives λ_n ≥ 0.

λ_n relate to the Taylor coefficients of log ξ(1/(1-z)) at z = 0. A zero off the line yields, by the symmetry ρ ↔ 1-ρ, a zero with |1 - 1/ρ| > 1; its contribution grows exponentially in n and oscillates in sign, which forces λ_n < 0 for some n (Li; Bombieri–Lagarias).

For Re ρ > 1/2, x^{ρ-1} lies in L²(0,1), so f ↦ ∫_0^1 f(x) x^{ρ-1} dx is a continuous linear functional. On each generator its value is a multiple of ζ(ρ)(θ^ρ - θ)/ρ, hence 0 if ζ(ρ) = 0, while on the constant 1 it is 1/ρ ≠ 0. So 1 is not in the closed span, contradicting density.
Explicit formula with |x^ρ| = x^{1/2} gives ψ(x) - x = O(√x log² x); partial summation gives π(x) - li(x) = O(√x log x). Converse via the Mellin transform of π - li.

The Mellin representation converges absolutely for Re(s) > 1/2 + ε under the bound, so 1/ζ is holomorphic there; conversely RH gives 1/ζ(s) ≪ |t|^ε on Re(s) ≥ 1/2 + ε and Perron gives the bound on M(x).
